reviews.text: 这不就是牢a所说的斩杀线吗？ 伟大与自由是精美包装的诱饵。低房价和永久产权的背后是持续吸血的房产税；免费医疗的背后是“短期残障”医疗保险；体面的西服和体香背后是街边的租衣店和便利店里贩卖的除臭剂。负债被打包成债券出售成为理财产品，当你最后撑不住了，流落街头只能捏着手里仅剩的家人合照，衣衫褴褛地严肃地愤怒地喊出一句“自由万岁，人权万岁！”时，旁边的年轻人只会拍一张照片发到网上，然后附赠一句“嘿，哥们儿真有节目效果！”。 蓝星上的边缘人物一直都存在，且大量的边缘人物被结构性体系挤压之下被“与世隔绝”了。这种结构性的系统不是大自然的产物，而是人为制造的庞大机器。机器犹如冷风吹过，不会错过任何一个人，也不会停下哪怕一刻。 也许就在此时此刻，我的头上也有着一片“灰暗角落”，聚集着老爷们需要的血包以及抛弃的垃圾。 最后， 敬人民，敬无名角落，敬混蛋老爷！

I'm really enjoying the gameplay, there is a lot of complexity and content but it lets you chose the rate at which you approach it instead of being forced to be on the knife's edge all the time. Thus it's unusually relaxing for such a hardcore game. There can be a lot of text, which some will like and some won't. You can skip this without any problems.

玩通了第一个剧情，兴致勃勃准备写点评价，结果点开一看评论区经典难民账号“1差评”。 明明这种黑色幽默式的太空朋克幻想剧情非常有意思，但是评论区大神依旧评价为“故作深奥”，我说哥们咱们就承认自己连这样水平线以上的剧情根本看不懂不就完事了？ 如此和题材紧密挂钩的剧情到你这8级号的嘴里直接零论据差评，我是制作组真要罚你把每个“故作深奥”的节点写个三百字剧情分析了。 脑子不会因为你假装清醒明智就突然出现在你的头颅里，哲思更不是像你一样牛头不对马嘴般喊叫就会扣在你头顶的。
真不错，结合现在的“斩杀线”玩这个，简直了，以前黑深残的那些剧情看不明白，感觉故作深奥，但是牢a的事情出来后，游戏里面的一切都是这么合情合理

Damn it. One time I purchased a trio of day-old croissants in a sealed cellophane bag from a local bakery. I was very excited to eat them, I knew they would be delicious. When I arrived home and set the bag on the counter I noticed a black spot on the bottom of one of the pastries. Somehow, when they had been bagged up a fly had gotten trapped inside with them. It was crushed now, between flaky crust and clear plastic. Some of it's legs had been broken off. It still writhed, weakly. Yesterday I watched a youtuber play this game as second monitor content. About 5 minutes in I immediately went and bought it. I played it nonstop for the next three hours, staying up later than I should have. It was great, I was fixated, it was hard to sleep that night. After a groggy day of work I was excited to play it again today. I noticed the game's banner depicted ships very unlike the ones in the game. Mottled, vague things with forward facing guns firing indistinguishable beams of color into each other. AI generated. It says it right there at the bottom of the page if I'd taken a second to read. So much of this game is good. There are so many simple systems that interact with each other in fascinating ways. Ship adjacency and module slots, building your fleet into a pattern that allows it to adapt and endure unknown numbers and configurations of enemies. I was only two runs into this game and already I was excited to see what new little fiddly mechanic would come along and shake up my current understanding of the game. I like the how the characters talk, so entrenched in this miserable future that they are essentially aliens (or were the conversations just generated?). I like how in the main menu, when the music picks up more randomized ships are spawned into the background (was the music generated?). I hate having to second guess everything. Is there motivation behind why a background looks a certain way, or why a character says something or is it just accidental noise? Does it matter if the game is fun to play? The other two croissants were probably fine, the fly was only squished into the one part, but I threw the whole bag away anyways. Go play Starsector I guess?

Space corporate dystopia roguelite deckbuilder, with translations from chinese that is understandable enough to play the game. There is a lot of dialogue if you don't mind reading through it all, mostly world building of this spacefaring ultra late-stage capitalistic society that treats human lives as worth less than pet food; all of it is skippable though and you can get right into the meat of the game. It is somewhat similar to backpack hero, that it is a single player game where you choose your path and gain per run items to place and modify. These pieces come in the shape of ships and their modules. The meta-progression is when you get enough currency to field a large starting deck (field of ships and modules) to easily deal with upcoming encounters. There are a lot of ships and modules to unlock, when you complete a successful run with them in hand, which will allow you to buy them with the currency you slowly collect each run. When you make a bad judgement call and fail a run, you can lose your ships which you have carefully procured. The difficulty seems harsh at first, but can be overcome by understanding the game mechanics. The game gives me a 'one more run' feel just like FTL did, even with the limited events currently in the game. I hope that there will be future updates or DLCs that will expand on this lore/universe.

游戏不错，激光大炮就是宇宙战舰的终极浪漫！ 文案作者看得出来有一定的文学哲学基础，既然如此，我也想说一点游戏外的略带严肃的话题：也就是文案展现出来的意识形态太过老旧了。 这类的反乌托邦未来完全是右翼文化或者说资本主义内部的反思产物， 尤其是类赛博朋克文化（高科技，低生活）其实根本就不是在反对资本主义，而是正认为“资本主义是唯一可行的未来”，以此作为叙事基础而做的悲观反思。这类反思思潮正集中在上个世纪70-90年代，而当时发生了什么，自然也不需要多说。我知道我们的很多年轻创作者还都受到那时开始的大量文艺作品滋养，依样画葫芦。但时至今日，我是说到了2026年这个时间点，还在加入到这类思潮中去，则有点略显过时了。 文案原文写道“人类的生理结构在太空全是问题，远航成本极高。人的个体寿命又太短，能健康活动的年份就那么点，不 得不只顾眼前。计划固然伟大，但远远超出了文明所能承受的极限。地球上的人们只是想活着，如果可能，活得好一点。” 这显然又是西方视角才能说出的话，而这样的话让“纤夫”来说则更加不合时宜，因为“愚公移山”从未考虑过在“我”这一辈子就把山移走，寿命从未成为问题，我方从未想过一人解决一个问题。 早在《神经漫游者》还未完成的六年前，也就是1978年，远在东方的三北防护林工程启动，计划长达七十多年分为八期项目一直持续到2050年，这绝不是一个人，或者一代人就可以完成，毛乌素、塞罕坝，一直到2024年的塔克拉玛干锁边完成，我们从未嫌弃个体寿命太短，一代人无法完成伟业。 我自己的科幻口味上，更加喜欢阿瑟克拉克，但是时至今日，我们国内的创作者应该要明白，什么才是属于中国自己的科幻创作，而不要再照本宣科那些老掉牙的东西，跟着落后的意识形态老调重弹。 既然“信封”的思考能力如此强，我这点小猪话应该也不算自顾自话。

This game was surprisingly good. I got it to scratch a space itch while waiting on the new Battlestar Galactica game, but I was really surprised! You play as a trio of people doing 'investigations' - looting the remains of surrounding failing corporate space - for a company called Residual Life. You get a cut of the value of whatever you salvage in each run. The gameplay is like FTL in its route-finding path, and like Gratuitous Space Battles for the actual battles, with a few added mechanics thrown in. Pros: The dialogue and plot are surprisingly thoughtful, though don't be surprised if a few characters are simply rambling lunatics. This is space, after all. I think the way they handle the difficulty in the game is the thing to highlight. There are 6 total corporations that make their own ships and equipment. The first one you can access has the cheapest and weakest ships. The second company is stronger, with a few top-tier ships, but the other 4 corporations are more-or-less equal in terms of ship strength. The challenge from the middle of the game onwards, is learning each corporation's core mechanics, and building a fleet to deal with them. The strongest ship in the game - by far - is fielded by the third boss of the game, NOT the final boss. The devs created a challenging game WITHOUT giving later opponents ships with bigger numbers. I think each corporation's ships demonstrate the corporation's mentality well. Sensaholic - a giant colloseum - uses a debuff called thermal softening. This is a stackable status that increases the next hit's damage by the number of stacks, and removes 1 stack, so 50 stacks on a ship would cause it to take 50 more damage, then remove 1 stack. In practice, this is a big comeback mechanic when facing Senseholic. You'll have their fleet almost beat, but with the softening stacked on your own ships, they start melting. Similarly, the Vacuum Noble corporation's ships have a very 'corporate' theme. Their ships have names like Limited Liability and Information Rent Seeker. They have a mechanic called energy budget. Each stack reduces received damage by 1% (max 30% damage reduction), but some weapons use these stacks to do more damage AND running out of energy budget will cause the related weapons to fire slower. This gives them a strong first-strike capability, which can take some getting used to, coming straight from fighting a faction that focused on comeback mechanics. As a player, you can take advantage of all these mechanics at once. Corporation modules are not restricted to being put on their own ships. Combining different modules is a key to getting through the waves of very strong fleets from the inner core toward the end of the game. There is a ship called BE-BOP. If you're good, there's not much grinding in the game. The only requirements to use a ship are a) find it as salvage and/or b) bring it back at least once, and have the money to buy it. The exceptions are 1 super-ship and 3 modules. They include a boss arena in the end/post game, so you can fight all the game's bosses over again without having to create a new playthrough. Cons: Some of the basic UI is gated behind a contract wager system, where you take certain benefits, but lose some of your share of the salvage, or you give up some functions, but gain a higher salvage reward. There's a 2x speed boost toggle button at the top of the screen you can only use if you take a contract that loses you 2% of your final share. To be fair, after the first few tasks, your salvage share stops mattering as much. Ultimately: I'd say watch a YouTube video to see if the mechanics and gameplay are to your taste; I think it was worth the money.

Weak translation, solid gameplay. The mechanics are slightlty obscure and the whole worldbuilding reads like it was written by a disgruntled Tencent employee (which I can relate to, as I am also a corporate peon), but the actual gameplay is solid. You'll build a fleet using pre-made ships, each ship having its own passive effect. Modules can be added to ship to combine with their passives, and ships can be placed on a large grid with ship placement being relevant. You want your fleet formation to maximize adjecency for some modules, but you also want to squeeze as many ships on your board as possible. The game follows a STS-like navigation, where you have to choose from a variety of combat encounters, events and shops. The meta progression is all about grinding money to buy more ships so you can create more fleets for a variety of situations. Fleets can be influenced with passive elements before leaving (Cores for buffs, wager contracts and pilot abilities to impact your profit margin either lowering it to make the game easier or heightening it to make the game harder). Fleet combat plays like an autobattler, on which you can use pilot abilities (mothership support) and move ships around in real time to impact the outcome, with a handy pause button you can use to read enemy abilities. The game has really good bones, and is very chinese in its implementation- UI could use some improvements and I'd love more ships\modules to play around with, but I've enjoyed it so far.

Its an alright little game. I have such delusions of grandeur for the game but as is, I would recommend it at half price. I wish the ship power levels weren't in such obvious tiers. Some more horizontal progression would go a long way to introduce some variety to the fleet compositions. I wish the VN elements had more bite to it and much less repetition. The eternal "visual novel curse" is in full effect here too. Since the writer fears the players could have skipped an important passage they repeat every interaction five times, so the player is less likely to read it all and skip dialogue, meaning there's higher chance an important passage is skipped so the writer repeats more dialogue over and over. And VNs that waste your time by making the player re-read passages suck. I wish i wouldn't feel like every background artworks for the hub departments were A.I. generated images with a mosaic filter slapped ontop. Once suspicion of AI assets being stealthily used sets in, it poisons the entire experience. Luckily the stops in the hub are short enough to forget about it once an expedition starts and thankfully the ships and space backdrops lack the "AI-feel".
